title: Soft-flush + preemptive interruptible generation: design notes
body:
Purpose:

This doc captures a proposed design for making token-streaming more responsive and robust by combining: (1) soft-flush heuristics, (2) preemptive interruptible generation, and (3) KV-cache-aware scheduling. We want lower tail latency for interactive workloads while avoiding quality regressions and minimizing wasted compute when requests are cancelled or re-routed.

Background / motivation:
- Current behavior: the runtime emits tokens in fixed chunks (X tokens / Y ms) and supports hard cancellation at request boundaries. This causes:
  - unnecessary latency for short responses when chunk size is tuned for throughput,
  - wasted GPU cycles when cancellations happen mid-kernel or mid-batch,
  - complex interactions with KV cache: when we interrupt and restart with cached KV state we may repeat work or mis-handle partial caches.

Key goals:
1) Reduce median and p95 response time for short interactive responses without drastically increasing per-token overhead.
2) Allow safe interruption of in-flight generation with an ability to provide a graceful partial output (soft flush) rather than only hard cancellation.
3) Keep KV-cache correctness and avoid cache pollution or inconsistency from preempted generations.
4) Make scheduling decisions (preempt vs finish) visible to higher layers (routing, console) for billing/analytics.

Constraints and non-goals:
- We will not change model tokenization semantics (tokens are still discrete). Partial-token byte-level streaming is out of scope for now.
- Hardware/kernel constraints: we must respect kernel-level execution windows (e.g., kernel that emits N tokens per launch). We can only preempt at safe preemption points the runtime exposes.

Definitions:
- soft-flush: emitting a best-effort partial completion to the client (e.g., current token boundary plus a small buffered suffix) when we choose to yield or prepare for preemption. This is tagged as non-final in the protocol so clients know more tokens may follow.
- preemptive interrupt: scheduler-triggered decision to stop continuing this request for now; can be voluntary (to improve cost/latency tradeoff) or forced (high-priority request arrives).
- safe preemption point: a state inside the runtime/kernel at which stopping further generation will not corrupt KV cache or leak uninitialized states (e.g., after KV write-back checkpoint).

Design overview (high level):
1) Add a soft-flush API primitive in the serving runtime: emit_soft_flush(metadata)
   - Runtime ensures flush occurs at a safe preemption point (or as close as possible).
   - Metadata includes: flush_type (time-based / token-count / delimiter), reason (scheduler_preempt | client_poll | kv_sync), and trace ids for observability.

2) Scheduler integration: preemption policy that considers:
   - request priority class (interactive vs batch),
   - estimated remaining tokens (from prompt heuristics + model length),
   - KV cache locality (hot cache => cheaper to continue),
   - current kernel occupancy and batch shape.

3) KV-cache-aware behavior:
   - Do not evict or commit partial KV entries until a generation completes a min-stable checkpoint.
   - When preempting, persist only the minimal necessary KV checkpoint to allow safe resume (e.g., attention key/val slices up to last emitted token).
   - Tag partial checkpoints as transient; GC policy reclaims them after T seconds if not resumed.

4) Cancellation semantics:
   - hard_cancel: client requests immediate termination; runtime returns a cancellation acknowledgment and best-effort partial soft-flush if available. Billing marks the request as cancelled and charges for work done.
   - interrupt_for_preemption: scheduler-initiated; runtime attempts soft-flush, records preemption metadata, and either suspends (keep partial KV) or finishes (commit KV) depending on config and cost calculus.

Flush policy heuristics (proposed):
- Multi-dimensional soft-flush trigger: flush when ANY of the following fire:
  * elapsed_since_last_emit > latency_target_ms / 2 AND next_kernel_expected > latency_target_ms (to avoid blocking on a long kernel),
  * emitted_tokens_since_last_flush >= soft_chunk_tokens (adaptive per-request),
  * incoming high-priority request needs preemption and this request is low priority,
  * delimiter token emitted (punctuation heuristics) when enable_delimiter_soft_flush = true.

- soft_chunk_tokens is adaptive: start with 2 tokens for interactive short prompts, back off to 8 tokens when model_mode == high-throughput. We derive starting point from historical per-route latency/cost metrics.

Partial-token semantics (clarify):
- We do not emit raw partial tokenizer bytes. Partial tokens here mean: if kernel produces sub-token logits or byte pieces internally, runtime waits until token-decoding boundary. We only ever send client-valid tokens.
- However we introduce an explicit "in-progress-token" boolean in stream frames. If set, client UI may show a spinner or in-place token anim until token finalization. This helps UX where soft-flush occurs mid-latency-window and we want to signal additional completion imminently.

Kernel and batching interplay:
- Kernels typically produce K tokens per kernel-launch. If K is large (e.g., 16 tokens), and latency_target is small, we should:
  1) prefer kernels with smaller K when request is interactive (via kernel selection heuristics), or
  2) allow kernel to run but plan a soft-flush at the first safe preemption point that kernel exposes (e.g., at internal token boundary).
- Batching: when many interactive small requests coalesce into a batch, soft-flush decisions are per-request but implementation triggers at batch sync points. The scheduler can choose to finish a few top-priority items in a micro-batch and soft-flush the rest.

State machine (simplified):
- states: queued -> running -> soft-flushed (suspended) -> resumed -> finished | cancelled
- transitions: running -> soft-flushed occurs when scheduler preempts; runtime stores transient KV checkpoint; running -> cancelled when client requests hard cancel.

Observability and billing hooks:
- Surface the following events in trace/log: soft_flush_emitted, preemption_requested, kv_checkpoint_saved, resume_from_checkpoint, hard_cancel_received. Each event includes token counters and elapsed time.
- Billing: if soft-flush leads to suspension and later resume, we charge for total compute across both segments. If preemption leads to immediate termination, charge for work done. Record reason tags for audit.

Examples / heuristics in practice:
- Short-chat use case: user prompt + expected 4-10 tokens. Set soft_chunk_tokens=2, latency_target=60ms. Prefers small kernels (K<=4) or schedules preemption after first token if other priority arrives.
- Long-generation use case (articles): soft-flush every 16 tokens or when hitting natural delimiter; but prefer to finish kernels to avoid quality issues.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Cost of saving transient KV checkpoints vs recompute cost if we tear down and later resume. Need telemetry to establish crossover point. Propose experiment: measure resume_cost / checkpoint_write_cost across top 5 model variants.
- UX contract for clients: how to represent in-progress tokens and soft-flush interim results (should SDK show them as final? probably not).
- Kernel API surface: we need kernel-level support to return safe_preemption_offsets within a kernel launch. Kernel teams must expose a compact descriptor.

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 0: telemetry & experiments (2 weeks): instrument current pipeline to measure kernel token granularity, cancellation latency, and KV checkpoint size and write time.
- Phase 1: runtime primitives (4 weeks): add emit_soft_flush, transient KV checkpoint store, and scheduler hooks. Expose observability events.
- Phase 2: policy rollout (3 weeks): deploy adaptive soft_chunk_tokens and preemption heuristics behind a route flag. Run A/B on interactive routes.
- Phase 3: kernel collaboration (ongoing): define kernel preemption descriptor and implement in 1-2 representative kernels.

TODOs (owners):
- [Asha] add telemetry dashboard for checkpoint write vs recompute (CON-3421).
- [Miguel] prototype transient KV store API and TTL cleanup.
- [Sara] design SDK signal for in-progress-token frames and update streaming protocol doc.
- [Devon] evaluate kernel preemption feasibility with XLA/cuDNN team.

Appendix: simulated trace (example):
- t=0: request R1 queued (interactive), t=5ms: kernel K1 launched (K=8 tokens), t=30ms: high-priority R2 arrives, scheduler requests preempt at next safe point, runtime computes soft_flush at token 2 boundary, emit_soft_flush -> client gets 2 tokens + in-progress flag, checkpoint KV up to t=30ms saved transiently, K1 aborted after token boundary, R1 moved to suspended pool, R2 scheduled immediately. If R1 resumes within TTL, resume uses checkpoint and re-enters kernel selection with smaller K.

This is a working draft. Comments requested from kernel, scheduler, and KV-cache owners.

References / related tickets:
- CON-3421: checkpoint vs recompute telemetry
- GH-rlw/serving#678: streaming framing changes (must not duplicate)
- Slack: runtime-arch thread 2025-09-03 for initial brainstorming

End of doc.
